p2.key:
(i) m/z 58: molecular ion, so Mr = 58 (e.g. C3H6O). m/z 43: fragment from loss of CH3 (58 − 15), i.e. CH3CO+ (or C3H7+).

(ii) A ≈ 1700–1750 cm−1: C=O. (No broad O–H band, so not an alcohol or acid.)

(iii) Only one signal (≈ 2.2 ppm) → all H atoms in one chemical environment, consistent with CH3 next to C=O (R–CO–CH3, 2.2–2.7 ppm). Compound: propanone, CH3COCH3 (not propanal, which would show 3 signals incl. ≈ 9.5 ppm).

(i) Two enantiomers as mirror images: the chiral C2 with H, OH, CH3 and C2H5, two bonds in the plane, one wedge and one dash; the second drawing is the mirror image (e.g. OH on a wedge in one and a dash in the other).

(ii) Pass plane-polarized light through a solution of each enantiomer (same concentration and path length). Each rotates the plane of polarization by the same angle but in opposite directions (one clockwise, one anticlockwise).

(i) H = 100 − 48.6 − 43.2 = 8.2 %. Moles: C 48.6/12.01 = 4.05; H 8.2/1.01 = 8.12; O 43.2/16.00 = 2.70. Divide by 2.70: 1.5 : 3 : 1 → ×2 → C3H6O2.

(ii) m/z 74: molecular ion [C3H6O2]+ (Mr = 74). m/z 45: COOH+ (loss of C2H5, 74 − 29).

(iii) A (very broad, 2500–3000 cm−1): O–H in a carboxylic acid. B (≈1700–1750 cm−1): C=O.

(iv) Propanoic acid, CH3CH2COOH.

(i) H–C(=O)–O–CH2–CH3 drawn with all bonds and H atoms shown. Name: ethyl methanoate.

(ii) Three signals: HCOO– H: singlet; –CH2–: quartet (next to CH3); –CH3: triplet (next to CH2).

(iii) Any one (explained): all 12 H atoms are equivalent, giving a single strong signal; the signal is upfield, away from most other signals (defined as 0 ppm); it is chemically inert/non-toxic and volatile, so easily removed from the sample.

2-Bromobutane, CH3CHBrCH2CH3, has a chiral C2 (bonded to H, Br, CH3 and C2H5). Draw two tetrahedral wedge–dash structures that are non-superimposable mirror images (enantiomers), with a mirror line between them — e.g. Br on a wedge in one and on a dash in the other.
